factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: The opportunity is anchored in a real, recurring MDR obligation: manufacturers must continuously connect heterogeneous post-market evidence to trend, risk, CAPA, and PSUR outputs. That is a concrete workflow problem rather than a generic AI use case, but official guidance standardizes much of the process and creates no vendor-exclusive control point.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Audit readiness, incomplete complaint lineage, and safety-reporting consequences make the underlying pain consequential, and lean QA/RA teams have a reasonable basis to pay for reduced review effort and fewer missing links. However, representative complaint volume, current preparation cost, and willingness to fund a separate layer instead of an existing QMS module or consultant remain unknown, so the strength and frequency of the paid pain are not yet established.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Paid onboarding plus subscription fits a validated regulated workflow and could produce recurring revenue, but the proposed pricing, 12-month payback, retention, and 55-80% gross-margin progression are assumptions. Customer-specific connectors, software validation, security, and qualified QA/RA review create a credible risk that implementation and support remain service-heavy; the illustrative founder-wealth path also requires 175 customers at PLN 60,000 ARR without a validated reachable denominator, CAC, churn, or sales cycle.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Small EU Class IIa/IIb manufacturers with lean teams and one to twenty device families form a coherent, focused beachhead with a shared regulatory job. The cited 38,000-plus European medtech-company count is far broader than this segment, though, and there is no sourced count of manufacturers with sufficiently fragmented evidence and budget, leaving the beachhead's economic depth uncertain.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: MasterControl and Greenlight Guru already market connected post-market, complaint, risk, CAPA, reporting, and traceability workflows, while Greenlight Guru states that more than 1,100 medtech companies use its platform. A deeper complaint-to-denominator lineage layer could win a narrow use case, but without a measured superiority or exclusive distribution position it is more likely to be treated as a feature or overlay than to dominate the beachhead.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A proven lineage engine could extend into other device classes, IVDs, PMCF and clinical-evidence workflows, additional reports, or other regulated geographies. Those adjacencies are logically available but not yet de-risked, and each adds regulatory nuance, validation burden, and direct competition from broader life-sciences suites.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Validated customer-specific lineage rules, embedded approvals, and accumulated audit history could create switching costs after deployment. The proposed extraction and drafting capabilities are reproducible, lawful reuse of health-related complaint data is constrained, and incumbents can add similar lineage features inside systems already holding the source records, so the prospective data and workflow moat is weak.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: End-to-end evidence lineage and audit exports could be materially clearer than spreadsheets or consultant workarounds, particularly for fragmented sources. No evidence yet shows a decisive reduction in review time, missing links, audit findings, or total cost, and incumbent products already claim connected feedback, risk, quality, and traceability, so a behavior-changing advantage remains a hypothesis.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Continuous MDR duties and the still-in-development EUDAMED vigilance and PMS module leave a current workflow gap, while recent MDCG guidance makes the cross-source job explicit. The obligations are not a new temporary opening, mature vendors already serve them, and future EUDAMED functionality could absorb some workflow steps, producing balanced rather than exceptional timing.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: A fixed-fee traceability assessment is a credible low-risk route to two design partners, and independent QA/RA consultants are a plausible trust-bearing referral channel. No consultant commitment, conversion rate, CAC, or repeatable sales process exists, and selling a separate regulated-data layer to cautious manufacturers is likely to be relationship-intensive and slow, making expansion to the customer count required by the economics difficult for this founder without a real channel.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's data-science background fits entity resolution and evidence normalization, AI can accelerate the build, and customer-owned regulatory decisions avoid the most dangerous autonomy claim. Nevertheless, GDPR-sensitive records, validated software, integrations, cybersecurity, domain review, contractual liability, and support around short vigilance clocks require qualified partners and operational coverage that are difficult to sustain with a five-hour-per-day founder and PLN 100,000 initial capital.

assumptions: The initial customer keeps every safety, reportability, submission, and approval decision with its qualified PRRC or QA/RA personnel.
At least a subset of small Class IIa/IIb manufacturers has fragmented source evidence and recurring PSUR work substantial enough to test a separate paid lineage layer.
The founder limits the first stage to two design partners and can contract qualified regulatory, validation, security, and support help within the stated capital and part-time constraints.
The product can integrate with existing QMS and source systems without requiring customers to replace their system of record.
Health-related complaint data can be processed under customer-approved GDPR, minimization, security, and controller-processor controls without relying on unrestricted cross-customer model training.
main_structural_strength: A legally required, continuous, audit-sensitive workflow gives the product a concrete recurring trigger, and the proposed lineage from raw complaint and service evidence through denominators, risk, CAPA, qualified approval, and PSUR output is narrower and more valuable than generic document drafting.
primary_score_limiter: The candidate has not established a sufficiently superior standalone control point or separate budget against QMS/PMS suites that already bundle complaints, risk, CAPA, reporting, and traceability, which constrains achievable pricing, distribution, retention, and domination potential.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: Established vendors already sell substantially overlapping connected workflows: MasterControl explicitly links post-market activity, feedback, issue analysis, risk, and core quality processes, while Greenlight Guru combines feedback, regulatory-reporting assessment, CAPA, risk, and traceability and reports adoption by more than 1,100 medtech companies.
highest_value_structural_change: Make independent QA/RA consultancies the primary customer and reseller through a validated multi-client partner edition that leaves each manufacturer's QMS as the system of record; one consultant relationship could supply regulatory trust, repeat deployments, and pooled implementation learning while avoiding a head-on full-suite replacement sale.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: Run paid pilots on representative manufacturer data and obtain a competitor-referenced before-and-after record covering PSUR preparation hours, missing-link and audit-quality improvement, onboarding and validation labor, support load, sales-cycle length, subscription conversion and renewal intent, together with signed consultant channel commitments and a sourced count of reachable target manufacturers.
